newsitem.title: GERMANY: German small shareholders stick out bourse fall.
newsitem.headline: German small shareholders stick out bourse fall.

text.p: Thousands of small shareholders, swept up in the dizzying climb of Germany's stock market over the past year, showed few signs of vertigo on Monday as the DAX blue-chip index came tumbling down in the wake of Wall Street.

More than a few seasoned stock traders have suggested that novice investors who got on board through popular flotations such as Deutsche Telekom and TV group Pro Sieben Media would get seasick and bail out as soon as the market fell.
Investment advisers for several German banks said that while a large number of sell orders had been taken from private investors there was no mass sell-off.
Harald Bochow, head of equity services at Berliner Volksbank, said most private investors had remained calm in light of the turbulence on the stock market.
"The small shareholder has grown up," he said.

If any lesson can be learned from Monday's rollercoaster ride as the DAX index of 30 blue-chip stocks plunged four percent at the opening, it is that small shareholders are more astute than expected and they are here to stay.

"I don't think the market is falling through the floor," said Rainer Koch, 28, a Frankfurt marketing manager who has been investing in shares for the past three years. "This is not a crash. It's really just a healthy correction."

Germany's DAX index, catching up to Friday's heavy losses on Wall Street, tumbled about four percent at the outset of bourse dealings, but recovered some lost ground later in the day to close at 4,078.60 points, down 1.79 percent.
Dealers said it was psychologically important that the DAX closed above the 4,000 mark, suggesting the German market could break away from Wall Street if U.S. shares continued to slide.

The DAX has surged some 55 percent since the beginning of the year and with the current low interest rate environment analysts expect the latest falls to provide the room needed to spark more growth over the next few months.

Wall Street on Friday posted the second largest point decline in a single day after the infamous "Black Monday" when on October 19, 1987 the Dow Jones Index plunged 22 percent in one day, ruining the fortunes of many investors.
The DAX is some 400 points below its all-time high of 4,477.70 points on July 31, but there are no signs of panic.
Wolfgang Sander, a product manager for a U.S. company in Frankfurt and a veteran dabbler in the stock market, monitored the day's dealings from his office.
"I've been investing in shares for 18 years and I've seen a few ups and downs," he said. "I wouldn't want to interpret more into this than is necessary."
Christoph Bruns, head of investment fund management at Union-Investment-Gesellschaft, said there was still plenty of money going into the market.
"The danger is not only that stock prices are falling, but that they could rise and you are not in the market," he said.
Direkt Anlage Bank, a unit of Hypo-Bank, said that by 10 a.m. more orders had been taken than usually come in during an entire day, with up to 60 percent of them for sell orders.
But at the end of the day the market got a boost from a wave of buy orders as prices for some stocks that had become too expensive began to look attractive.
